Golden-winged sunbirds (Drepanorhynchus reichenowi) exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in body mass, a trait commonly observed among nectarivorous passerines. Adult females typically attain an ultimate wet weight of 13.7 grams [Wwi = 13.7 grams], while their male counterparts reach a substantially larger adult body mass of 15.7 grams [Wwi = 15.7 grams], a difference that likely reflects the competitive demands of territory defense. At the onset of life, hatchlings emerge at a modest initial wet weight of just 2.02 grams [Ww0 = 2.02 grams], a value consistent with the altricial developmental mode characteristic of most oscine birds. This neonatal mass represents approximately thirteen percent of the female adult mass, a ratio that implies a considerable parental investment in rapid growth during the nestling phase. Field records from the highland forests of East Africa, where this species is endemic, indicate that the incubation period is relatively brief. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] hatch after an age at birth of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a duration comparable to that reported for the related sunbird Kurochkinegramma hypogrammicum. The thermal environment during this critical developmental window is a key determinant of embryonic success and subsequent chick viability.

Under the elevated thermoregulatory demands typical of active foraging periods in this species, when body temperature reaches 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental trajectory accelerates considerably. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at an age of 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a remarkably short nestling period that aligns with values documented for other small-bodied nectivores at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid transition from brooded chick to fledgling minimizes the time spent vulnerable to predation in the nest. Comparative data from the congeneric Kurochkinegramma hypogrammicum support this timing, suggesting that developmental rates are phylogenetically conserved within this clade. The achievement of nutritional independence follows shortly after fledging, as juveniles begin to exploit floral nectar sources under the guidance of attending adults. This accelerated life-history schedule imposes significant energetic costs on the provisioning parents, who must deliver a continuous supply of arthropod prey and nectar to sustain the high growth rate of the nestlings.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, is reached surprisingly early in this species. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which reflects the active metabolic state during the breeding season, the time since birth at puberty is documented at 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching]. This represents an exceptionally rapid maturation period, suggesting that individuals may begin gamete production before completing full somatic growth. The physiological mechanisms underlying this precocious gonadal activation likely involve a combination of high basal metabolic rates and abundant nectar resources that provide the necessary energetic surplus for reproductive tissue development. Such rapid attainment of reproductive potential is unusual among Afrotropical passerines of similar body size, most of which delay puberty until several months after fledging. The selective pressures driving this accelerated schedule may include intense competition for high-quality territories and the need to capitalize on brief seasonal peaks in floral nectar availability, which constrain the window for successful breeding.

First reproduction, representing the initiation of the first brood, occurs considerably later than puberty in the Golden-winged sunbird. Measurements indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 1.3 years after hatching [tR = 1.3 years after hatching] when individuals are maintained at an active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and the first successful reproductive attempt is a common pattern among small passerines, often attributed to the time required to secure a breeding territory, acquire foraging skills sufficient to support offspring, and develop the necessary social bonds with a mate. The interval of roughly 437 days from hatching to first clutch suggests that these sunbirds invest substantial time in post-fledging learning and territory establishment. Such deferred first reproduction is energetically strategic, allowing young birds to maximize their body condition before committing to the high metabolic demands of egg production and parental care. This life-history trait is consistent with a slow-paced reproductive strategy relative to the rapid developmental milestones observed earlier.

The maximum documented lifespan for the Golden-winged sunbird, recorded in field studies of marked individuals, extends to 8 years [am = 8 years] under the thermal conditions characteristic of their active physiological state at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is relatively substantial for a passerine of its size and is likely facilitated by the predictable year-round availability of nectar resources in its montane habitat. Annual reproductive output is constrained by this long lifespan and the delayed onset of first breeding. Females produce approximately 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches annually], with each clutch containing a single egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing a single egg], a modest fecundity that is typical of tropical highland specialists. Basal metabolic rate measurements provide insight into the energetic basis of this life history: resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 25.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 25.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively high metabolic rate, combined with low annual fecundity and extended lifespan, positions the Golden-winged sunbird as a slow-living species that invests heavily in individual survival and the success of each rare reproductive event.
